title: Meridian - Secure image provisioning & GPU driver validation
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-09-15 16:00 UTC | Duration approx 58 min | Recording: yes
Attendees: Jordan Keller (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Liam Ortega (Redwood SE), Rosa Chen (Meridian), Matt Hollis (Meridian), Diego Valdez (Meridian), Sara Ibrahim (Meridian)
Shared artifacts: playbook link: https://redwood.internal/meridian-playbook (shared after call), bundle checksum sheet (drive link), offline licensing spec (PDF).

00:00 Jordan Keller: OK, thanks everyone for joining, we'll kick off, um, this is the runtime and image provisioning deep-dive for Meridian's air‑gapped site. The plan — Priya will run through the signed bundle flow and then Liam will walk kernel/driver validation and perf expectations.
00:28 Rosa Chen: Awesome, quick note — we've got both our security and procurement folks on the line, so if we pause for contract/licensing bits that's fine. Also we are on a fairly locked down subnet, everything must be scp/usb delivery, no direct internet.
00:45 Priya Shah: Great, that's expected. We'll cover artifact signing, hmac/checksums, and an attestation step that runs during install. There are a couple of options — manifest-only signature versus fully-signed image.
01:20 Matt Hollis: Clarify please — by "fully-signed image" do you mean the whole tarball is signed with an RSA signature we verify locally? Or do you do chunked signing for large artifacts?
01:40 Priya Shah: We currently ship a signed tar.gz with a detached rsa sig plus an SHA256 checksum file. For very large bundles we can support chunked checksums (and an indexed manifest) so clients can stream-verify. In air‑gapped installs we recommend detached signature + checksum in the same artifact bundle.
02:10 Diego Valdez: And how does the license activation work? We can't phone home — do we use a HSM token or a license file that we upload during install?
02:30 Liam Ortega: There are two supported modes: a signed license file bound to a machine-id and an offline activation key. The license file is generated by Redwood using the customer's activation public key — you drop it into /etc/redwood/license.json and the local agent verifies signature with the embedded public key in the bundle. For extra assurance we can do license notarization via a per-bundle attestation token that you ship on a USB.
03:05 Sara Ibrahim: For procurement, is the offline license file replaceable mid-term? We may need to rotate keys or rehost.
03:20 Jordan Keller: Yes, license replacement and rotation is supported. We'll supply a key rotation runbook in the playbook. There's an API (for online customers) and a signed rotation bundle for air‑gapped sites. We'll include sample commands and an example agent output in the doc.
03:52 Rosa: Ok, let's talk GPU drivers — we're targeting Nvidia A40s and a couple of older P4s in staging. Our kernel is RHEL 8.7.
04:10 Priya: RHEL 8.7 is supported; for A40 we recommend driver 525+ and the matching CUDA that matches the runtime. There are two approaches: install vendor driver packages on host (rpm/deb) or deliver precompiled kernel modules in the Redwood bundle.
04:40 Matt: Precompiled modules sound tempting but curious about kernel ABI mismatches. We prefer host-managed drivers if possible.
05:00 Liam: Host-managed is the safest for ABI-stable environments. For locked-down infra we created a driver install shim: a script that verifies the host kernel version, compares it to a compatibility matrix in the bundle, and either instructs operators to install the vendor RPM or falls back to our prebuilt module. But the prebuilt route requires exact kernel release matching — we've seen float-by-one patch mismatches break module loading.
05:40 Diego: Can you run a small script to check kernels across hundreds of hosts? We need automation for fleet validation before install.
05:55 Priya: Yes, our offline bundle includes a small probing utility (binary) that reports uname -r, glibc, and kernel headers available. It generates a CSV of host fingerprints you can import into your inventory. We can share the probe tool source under NDA.
06:30 Unlabeled Speaker 1: (inaudible)
06:45 Jordan: Switching to runtime perf — expected latency/throughput with KV cache warm vs cold. Priya, you want to run numbers?
06:55 Priya: Sure. Baseline: single-A40, gpt-like model 7B-ish, unquantized FP16 path, cold KV cache, we see median token latency around 40–55 ms per token in our lab with continuous batching disabled. With the KV cache warm and batch size of 8 (concurrent requests), median per-token latency drops to ~18–22 ms. Your workload distribution matters — lots of short chats benefit from prefix cache.
07:30 Rosa: Our use-case is short-form Q&A internal docs, so most requests are <120 tokens but high qps. Latency matters, but cost also. Any quantization options for A40 we should consider?
07:50 Priya: A40 supports int8/4 quant on certain kernel paths — Redwood Optimize will recommend a quant profile. For A40, int8 gives ~1.7x speedup with minor quality hits for many workloads. We provide a quantization report in the playbook with sample outputs and a delta matrix.
08:20 Matt: Do quantized models still use the same kernel modules or require special operator drivers?
08:35 Liam: No extra kernel-level drivers. Quantization is an inference engine-level optimization; it sits in user-space and uses standard CUDA kernels (or custom fused kernels). The exception is when you use vendor-provided integer primitives that need a certain CUDA toolkit minimum — that's documented in the compatibility matrix.
09:05 Diego: On batching — you mentioned continuous batching earlier. Is that safe for low-latency short requests?
09:20 Priya: Continuous batching groups in-flight tokens into micro-batches to improve GPU throughput while trying to satisfy latency SLOs. For chatty short requests we cap micro-batch windows to 5–10 ms to avoid latency regression. There's a policy param in the runtime config you can tune per model/route.
09:55 Rosa: Any guidance for batch policy defaults for short Q&A?
10:05 Priya: Default we choose conservative 10 ms micro-batch, max batch 16 for A40 pools. If you need sub-50ms p90, we'd lower to 2–5 ms and accept lower throughput. We'll include tuned examples in the playbook.
10:35 Matt: Let's pivot to artifact delivery — we need a tamper-evident chain for image exchange between our central build facility and the air‑gapped site. What's Redwood's recommended flow?
10:55 Liam: Recommended: 1) Build artifacts in your secure CI, produce manifest + per-file SHA256. 2) Sign manifest with your org key. 3) Pack an OCI-like bundle (signed). 4) Transfer by physically shipped USB or secure courier. 5) Local verifier runs bundle-verify which checks signatures, checksums, and optionally verifies a timestamp from the build system. We support signing with both RSA and ed25519.
11:35 Rosa: How do we handle incremental updates? We don't want to ship the full 120GB bundle for small runtime patches.
11:50 Priya: We support delta bundles — binary diffs with their own signed manifests. The installer can apply deltas if the base hash matches. We also provide a prefetcher you can run offline to stage hot prefixes to warm the KV cache before traffic starts.
12:20 Diego: Prefetcher—does it require secret keys? We can't let it leak model weights.
12:35 Liam: The prefetcher works entirely locally; it uses the signed bundle and extracts hot tokens (prefixes) to populate the KV cache file. It never calls home. The prefetch cache is encrypted with a key included in the signed license bundle so only your hosts can decrypt it.
13:05 Matt: About encryption — are model weights encrypted at rest in the bundle? If someone intercepts the USB they could try to extract files.
13:20 Priya: Yes, model artifacts are encrypted with AES-256 GCM inside the bundle; the decryption key is included in a license envelope signed to your account. Without the envelope the extract step fails. We also provide an option for HSM-backed key wrappers if the site provides an HSM.
13:55 Rosa: Nice. On verification tooling — can we run the bundle-verify inside our restricted env? It requires openssl right?
14:10 Liam: The verifier is a static linked binary that includes crypto libs—no external dependencies. It outputs a human readable report and a machine readable JSON (we can produce a CSV too). For high-security sites we provide an attestation mode which will additionally produce a signed log entry you can ship to your audit system.
14:45 Unlabeled Speaker 1: (overlap)
15:00 Jordan: Side question from procurement — what's the offline SLA? If the onsite installs fail, how quickly can we get a support window?
15:15 Jordan Keller: For Private deployments we have enterprise SLAs: support phone, 24x7 on-call, and an on‑site escalation path depending on the contract tier. For air‑gapped installs we offer managed transfer options (we can sign and ship bundles) on an agreed schedule. We'll include an SLA excerpt in the next email.
15:45 Sara Ibrahim: Great. Back to kernel modules — we want to avoid compiling on site. How do you validate that prebuilt modules match our custom kernel patches?
16:10 Liam: We ask you to provide the exact kernel config and the kernel-headers used at build time. We build modules against your exact kernel and store the kernel release string in the bundle metadata. The installer checks for an exact match; if it doesn't match it will not attempt insmod and will fail safe with a clear error and remediation steps.
16:45 Diego: Could you add a "compatibility fuzz" option? For labs where patch levels differ we might accept small ABI mismatches.
17:00 Priya: We do have a permissive flag for lab installs that attempts to probe and try insmod, but it's not recommended for production — it can cause subtle instability. We'll note that in the playbook as a lab-only setting.
17:25 Rosa: Performance testing — we want a deterministic benchmark for predeploy. How should we replicate your lab numbers?
17:40 Priya: We'll give you a reproducible benchmark harness. Steps: install bundle, run our stress harness with a fixed seed, disable background processes, run a 60-minute steady-state with controlled concurrency. The harness outputs p50/p90/p99 and token throughput. We'll attach the harness and expected golden numbers in the playbook.
18:10 Matt: Any known gotchas with NFS or SAN storage for the model store?
18:25 Liam: Yes — latency and read contention matter. We recommend local NVMe for hot models and NFS for cold archives. If you're forced to use network storage, use a local read cache to avoid per-token I/O. We'll include sample fstab and systemd cache services in the repo.
18:55 Diego: Regarding KV cache eviction — how is that persisted across restarts?
19:10 Priya: KV cache is a memory-backed LRU with an on-disk snapshot option. On graceful shutdown we persist a compacted snapshot; on cold boot we can warm from a supplied snapshot in the bundle. For full cold starts we have a warmup tool that can run in background and gradually fill the cache.
19:45 Rosa: How big are those snapshots typically?
19:55 Priya: For a 7B model with typical prefix use they range 200–800 MB. For larger models snapshots can be multiple GBs. We include compression by default.
20:20 Matt: Security question — do you support SAML/SSO for the admin console in air‑gapped mode?
20:35 Jordan: Admin console can be run offline and supports SAML with a local IdP — we provide a dockerized IdP shim for isolated networks or you can integrate with existing on-prem IdP. Audit logs are local and we support long term retention to your syslog.
21:00 Rosa: Ok, practical timeline — we want to run a small pilot on 3 nodes next month. What do you need from us?
21:15 Priya: For pilot we need: kernel versions + headers, hardware inventory (gpu model/firmware), a small acceptance test plan, and access to a secure courier for bundle transfer. We'll produce a pilot bundle and a verification script.
21:40 Jordan: I'll follow up with a checklist and the pilot SOW.
21:50 Diego: One more edge case — what if our procurement won't accept USB delivery for security reasons? We might use a dedicated sealed transfer machine on site.
22:05 Liam: That's fine — we support a sealed transfer method (Airlock) where you hand us an encrypted disk image and we return a signed image. There's a documented HSM flow for that in the playbook.
22:30 Rosa: Great. A couple of quick clarifications then we can wrap.
22:40 Matt: On the kernel validation script output — can it produce a single pass/fail code for automation?
22:55 Priya: Yes it exits 0 on pass and non-zero on fail and emits a short machine-readable summary. We'll include examples and a Jenkins pipeline snippet.
23:15 Unlabeled Speaker 1: (muffled)
23:30 Priya: Also, about firmware — we require vendor driver + firmware compat checks for A40; firmware mismatch can lead to subtle perf cliffs. Please provide firmware revision.
23:50 Rosa: We'll add that to the inventory.
24:05 Jordan: Let's capture action items and next steps.
24:20 Priya: Action item: Priya to send the signed bundle playbook (redwood-playbook-meridian-v1.0.pdf) and the probe binary under NDA.
24:35 Liam: Action item: Liam to produce a kernel compatibility matrix for RHEL 8.7 and match against A40/525 driver.
24:50 Jordan: Action item: Jordan to send pilot SOW and SLA excerpt to Sara and cc procurement.
25:05 Diego: Action item: Meridian (Rosa) to provide kernel headers, firmware versions, and hardware inventory (CSV).
25:20 Sara Ibrahim: Action item: Sara to review procurement timelines and share any contract constraints by next week.
25:40 Rosa: We'll try to get that inventory by 2026-09-22.
26:00 Jordan: Quick recap — we'll share the playbook, tooling, a probe binary, pilot SOW and a sample license rotation runbook. Any blockers?
26:20 Matt: Not on our side. Slight concern — time to provision modules if you need to rebuild them for our kernels. What's the typical turnaround?
26:35 Liam: For a new kernel we can produce a per-site module build within 3 business days if we have headers and a clean build environment. For complex custom kernels it can be longer.
27:00 Diego: Performance expectations for pilot — what p90 should we target?
27:15 Priya: For pilot A40s with quant int8 and micro-batching tuned, p90 token latency around 20–30 ms is realistic for the 7B model. We'll include the golden numbers.
27:40 Unlabeled Speaker 1: (soft)
28:00 Jordan: All right, thanks everyone. We'll email the artifacts and set a follow-up checkpoint for one week after you receive the pilot bundle.
28:20 Rosa Chen: Thanks, appreciate it.
28:28 Meeting closed.
summary: Redwood and Meridian reviewed air‑gapped image provisioning, signed bundles, offline licensing modes, and GPU driver validation. Discussed delivery methods (USB/sealed transfer), verification tooling, kernel module strategies, KV cache warmup/prefetch, batching/quantization trade-offs, and pilot requirements. Action items include playbook delivery, probe binary, kernel compatibility matrix, pilot SOW, and inventory from Meridian.
